“… freedom, fleeing the horrors of civil war and never to return, withdrew beyond the Rhine and the Tigris.”
Bella pares superis facient civilia divos —
Mortalia nulli Sunt curate deo. Cladis tamen huius habemus Vindicatam, quantam terris dare numina fas est: Bella pares superis facient civilia divos.
“No god cares for the fate of mortals. Yet the gods have paid the penalty for this disaster, as far as gods can make amends to men: civil war will make the deified dead equal to the gods above.”
H. Bung — Hubertus Bung (1908–1981), jurist and pupil of Schmitt.
Confusion with my namesake in Tübingen — Carlo Schmid.
The first letter from Herbert Lemmel—see above, note to p. 4—to Schmitt reached him in 1948 on a Russian postcard addressed to:
“Professor Carl Schmidt, French Zone, Tübingen am Neckar (Württemberg).”

It was therefore delivered in Tübingen to Württemberg councillor of state and professor Karl Schmid, who at that time had not yet begun calling himself “Carlo.” Schmid forwarded it to Plettenberg with a covering letter on stationery headed “Staatsrat Prof. Dr. Karl Schmid,” RW 265 no. 8725/2:
I assume that the writer of the enclosed letter was trying to reach you rather than me, and I am therefore sending his letter on to you.

Schmitt and Schmid knew one another personally from meetings at the Academy for German Law and from a wartime journey Schmitt made to France, during which they met in Lille, where Schmid was serving as a military judge.
See Schmitt’s letter to Nette of 29 June 1980, Deutsches Literaturarchiv Marbach, Nette papers, HS 948460.
the fish by Gilles, the Leviathan by Nay, the magnificent diamond by Nay — Paintings by Werner Gilles and Ernst Wilhelm Nay (1902–1968) which Schmitt owned and particularly loved.
The complete letter is published in BW GJ, pp. 99–101.
Jünger — Friedrich Georg Jünger, Griechische Götter. Apollon, Pan, Dionysos, Frankfurt am Main 1943. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 22251.
Non intelligor ulli — In a letter written during his exile on the Black Sea, Ovid complains:
Barbarus hic ego sum, quia non intelligor ulli.
“Here I am the barbarian, because no one understands me.”
Charles Péguy — (1873–1914), French writer and representative of the Catholic revival.
“the highly educated Swiss” — Jacob Burckhardt. See below, notes to pp. 105 and 272.
“like that Serenissimus” — During the Berlin uprising of 1848, the Prussian king Friedrich Wilhelm IV is said to have shouted to the rebels:
“But they are not allowed to do that.”
to Nette — A draft of the letter dated 26 December 1947 survives among Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 29474.
J. K. — Josef Kohler (1849–1919), professor of civil law, philosophy of law, and criminal law at Berlin’s Friedrich Wilhelm University.
Schmitt attended Kohler’s lectures in 1907, during his first semester. Decades later he described him in his notes “1907 Berlin.” See Schmittiana I, 1988, pp. 15–16.
You Can’t Go Home Again — Title of a novel by Thomas Wolfe.
Samuel Butler, Erewhon — Samuel Butler, Erewhon; or, Over the Range, London 1872 and later editions. German edition: Erewhon oder jenseits der Berge, Frankfurt am Main 1994, pp. 123 ff.
To R. Smend — Letter published in BW Smend, p. 121.
reply from my childhood friend Kluxen — This letter is missing from the surviving Kluxen correspondence among Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 nos. 7909–7928.

Fritz Brust — (1884–?), probably a fellow student. In 1909 he received his doctorate in Strasbourg with the dissertation Die Ästhetik der Musik in neueren Kunsttheorien und das Problem ihrer Allgemeingültigkeit.
καὶ ἡ θάλασσα οὐκ ἔστιν ἔτι — “And the sea is no more.” Revelation 21:1, Greek New Testament.
Sors de l’enfance — A quotation from Jean-Jacques Rousseau, La Nouvelle Héloïse, Part V. The first letter begins:
“Leave childhood behind, my friend, wake up; do not surrender your whole life to the long sleep of reason. The years are passing; you have only enough left to become wise.”
Schmitt had already quoted this in 1922 in “Schatten Gottes.” See Tb 1921–24, p. 416.
W. Weber’s legal opinion — Werner Weber, Die Rechtslage des Johannishospitals in Leipzig (legal opinion), Leipzig 1948.
Joseph Kaiser’s dissertation — Joseph H. Kaiser, Die politische Klausel der Konkordate, doctoral dissertation in law, Tübingen 1947.

Saint Séverin, the saint of 8 January — The feast day of Saint Severinus of Noricum is not 8 January but 19 January. The eighth of January was the date of his death, in the year 482. He therefore did not live around the year 500.
Severinus’s political and spiritual work in the Danube frontier region, which Rome had long since abandoned, attracted considerable attention in his own time.
Lavelle — Louis Lavelle (1883–1951), La présence totale, Paris 1934; German translation: Die Gegenwart und das Ganze. Entwurf einer Philosophie des Seins und der Teilhabe, Düsseldorf 1952.

R. Capitant — René Capitant (1901–1970), French jurist, political scientist, and politician; member of the Resistance and minister in de Gaulle’s government in exile. He had known Schmitt in Berlin since 1931.
petite dentelle de Vénise — Fine lacework from Burano, the island in the Venetian lagoon.
“I have defied the Escaveçades of fate …” — This and the following sentences paraphrase Schmitt’s “Song of the Sixty-Year-Old” at the end of ECS. See also Gedichte, pp. 5–7.
Nam potenti et fido amico plus praesidii habet … — Correctly:
Nam potenti et fido amico niti plus praesidii habet …
“For relying on a powerful and faithful friend gives a person greater protection than most arts and intrigues.”
Francis Bacon, De dignitate et augmentis scientiarum, in The Works of F. Bacon, edited by James Spedding, Robert Leslie Ellis, and Douglas Denon Heath, vol. II, London 1857, p. 463.
“The servant glides …” — Quotations from Erewhon. See above, note to p. 57.
illum opportet crescere, istum autem minui — “That one must increase, while this one must decrease.”
John 3:30 in the Vulgate actually reads:
illum opportet crescere, me autem minui.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
“reaches up to the divine” — See Mozart, The Magic Flute:
“Man and woman, woman and man, Reach up toward the divine.”
“more animal than any animal” — See Goethe, Faust, in Goethes Werke (Hamburg edition), vol. 3, Munich 1972, p. 17, lines 285–286:
“He calls it reason and uses it alone To become more animal than any animal.”
Werner Blischke — (1917–1984), pupil of Schmitt and jurist, later a senior official in the administration of the German Bundestag.
At the beginning of 1945 Schmitt took Blischke and his wife into his house in Schlachtensee after their own home had been destroyed by bombing.
Alfred Döblin defines utopia … — In Alfred Döblin, Schriften zu Ästhetik, Poetik und Literatur, Olten and Freiburg im Breisgau 1989, p. 367.
Caspary’s book — The book Die Maschinenutopie, which Schmitt owned, was published not in 1930 but in 1927.
“the happiness of the gnat, à la Rossini” — An allusion to the popular Italian song “Il valzer del moscerino.”
ἄτοπον — The placeless; that which has no place.
μεταβολή, ἐναντίον — See above, note to p. 29.
οὔτε διακρίνεται οὔτε συγκρίνεται — Correctly: … συγκρίνεται; “it is neither separated nor combined,” Plato, Parmenides, 157a.

To H. P. Ipsen … — Schmitt is probably referring here to Hans Peter Ipsen, “Deutsche Gerichtsbarkeit unter Besatzungshoheit (Einwirkungen der Besatzung auf den gerichtlichen Rechtsschutz gegen deutsche Hoheitsakte in der britischen Besatzungszone),” in Jahrbuch für internationales und ausländisches öffentliches Recht, 1948, pp. 87–114.
qui mutant corda hominum et gentium — “Who move the hearts of men and nations.”
See Schmitt’s condolence card to Jünger dated 31 January 1945, reproduced in M. Tielke, Der stille Bürgerkrieg, Berlin 2007, pp. 133–134, figs. 5 and 6.
The wording sounds Biblical or patristic, but no source has been found. It was probably Schmitt’s own.
Video vestigia ineuntium, non exeuntium — Correctly:
video vestigia introeuntium, exeuntium autem vestigia non video.
“I see many tracks going in, but I see none coming out.”
These are the words spoken by the fox outside the lion’s cave in Aesop’s fable.
